string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and one of its most important historical and cultural cities. Located in northern China, Beijing has served as the capital of several Chinese dynasties, including the Yuan, Ming, and Qing. The city is famous for landmarks such as the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and the Summer Palace. The Great Wall can also be visited from areas near Beijing. Today, Beijing is a major centre of government, education, culture, and technology. It is home to many universities, museums, and research institutions. The city combines traditional Chinese architecture with modern transportation and urban development.

Shanghai is a major international city located on the eastern coast of China, near the mouth of the Yangtze River. Originally an important trading port, Shanghai developed rapidly during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Today, it is a leading centre for finance, commerce, shipping, and technology. The Bund is famous for its historic waterfront buildings, while Pudong is known for modern skyscrapers such as the Shanghai Tower and the Oriental Pearl Tower. Shanghai also has a rich cultural life, with museums, theatres, traditional neighbourhoods, and diverse cuisine. Its extensive metro system connects many parts of this large and economically important city.

Chongqing is a major municipality in southwestern China, situated near the meeting point of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. The city is known for its mountainous landscape, steep streets, bridges, and distinctive urban architecture. Chongqing developed as an important transportation and commercial centre because of its river connections. During the Second World War, it served as the wartime capital of China. Today, Chongqing is a significant centre for manufacturing, logistics, and regional development. It is also famous for its spicy hot pot cuisine. Popular attractions include Hongya Cave, the Three Gorges region, and the Dazu Rock Carvings located within the municipality.

Tianjin is a major port municipality in northern China, located near the Bohai Sea and southeast of Beijing. The city developed as an important trading and transportation centre because of its position along the Hai River and its access to the coast. During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, foreign concessions influenced parts of its architecture and urban development. Today, Tianjin is an important centre for manufacturing, shipping, education, and commerce. Visitors can explore the Five Great Avenues area, the Tianjin Eye observation wheel, and traditional streets featuring local crafts and food. Tianjin is also known for its distinctive snacks and historical connections with modern Chinese industry.
